'''''Aloe marlothii''''' (also known as the '''mountain aloe''' or the '''flat-flowered aloe''') is a large, single-stemmed Southern African [[aloe]] of rocky places and open flat country, occasionally growing up to {{convert|6|m}} tall.

==Description==
[[File:Aloe Marlothii,Huntington Desert Garden.jpg|thumb|left|''Aloe marlothii'' in flower, showing the uniquely horizontal racemes of the [[inflorescence]]]] 
[[File:Aloe marlothii - Mountain Aloe - South Africa 2.JPG|thumb|left|Like many aloe species, ''Aloe marlothii'' is more spiny when it is small and vulnerable to grazing.]]
Named after [[Rudolf Marloth]], a German-born South African botanist, this species of aloe has an especially large robust head of stiff, grey-green leaves. These leaves can be up to {{cvt|1.8|m}} long, {{cvt|30|cm}} wide,<ref>{{cite journal | last= Reynolds | first= G. W. | date= 1935 | title= Aloe marlothii - Some Forms and Hybrids | journal= Journal of the Botanical Society of South Africa | issue= 21 | page= 7 }}</ref> and about {{cvt|4|cm}} thick, and usually densely covered in short spines on the convex lower surfaces and less so on the concave upper surfaces. Like many other [[arborescent]] aloe species, this aloe is more spiny when it is small and as it becomes taller and less vulnerable to grazing, it loses many of the spines from its leaf surfaces. It normally has a trunk densely covered by the withered old leaves.

The [[inflorescence]] is a much-branched panicle with up to 30 or exceptionally 50 racemes. Flower colour varies a great deal, and ranges from yellow through orange (most common) to bright red. Flowering takes place through the winter months, as is the case with most aloes.

The distinctively horizontal branches of its inflorescence is an easy way to distinguish this species from other aloes. For this reason it is sometimes known as the '''flat-flowered aloe'''. However, the type known as ''Aloe spectabilis'', has taller, less horizontal inflorescences. The densely packed flowers all tend to point upwards from the [[raceme]].<ref>{{Cite web |url= http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantab/aloemarloth.htm|title=''Aloe marlothii'' {{!}} PlantZAfrica.com |website=www.plantzafrica.com |access-date=2017-08-01}}</ref>

When not in flower, it is easily confused with the closely related ''[[Aloe excelsa]]'' (Zimbabwe aloe), and with the similar-looking ''[[Aloe ferox]]'' (Cape aloe) and ''[[Aloe africana]]'' (African aloe) species to the south.<ref>{{Cite web |url= http://davesgarden.com/guides/articles/view/212/|title=Introduction to Tree Aloes, part 1: the solitary, unbranched species - Dave's Garden |website=davesgarden.com |access-date=2017-08-01}}</ref>

==Distribution==
Its distribution ranges from the [[Klipriviersberg Nature Reserve]] in [[Johannesburg]], through eastern [[Botswana]], northwards over the [[Soutpansberg]] to [[Zimbabwe]] and [[Malawi]] and eastwards through [[Eswatini]] and [[Mozambique]] to the coast. Within this range, it is especially common in mountainous areas, which led it to be known as the '''mountain aloe'''.

This species grades through intermediate forms into ''Aloe spectabilis'' [[G. W. Reynolds|Reynolds]] of [[KwaZulu-Natal]].{{cn|date=June 2025}} ''Aloe marlothii'' used to form natural hybrids with some 30 or more species.{{cn|date=June 2025}}
